paragraphs.text: For most of recorded history, signing was treated as gesture rather than language: a system of pictures made in the air, useful for the deaf and of no interest to anyone studying how language works. The assumption survived into the twentieth century and was overturned by a single line of research. A linguist working at an American college in the late 1950s began describing the signing used by his students with the tools normally applied to speech, and found that it had the properties those tools were built to detect. The finding was resisted for years, partly because it implied that a century of educational policy had been built on a mistake.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The decisive discovery was that signs are built from parts. Just as a spoken word is assembled from a small inventory of sounds, a sign is assembled from a handshape, a location on or near the body, a movement, and the orientation of the palm. Change one of these and the meaning changes, exactly as changing one sound turns one word into another. That is the property linguists look for when deciding whether something is a language rather than a code, and signing has it. A pair of signs that differ only in where the hand is placed are as distinct to a fluent signer as two words differing in a single vowel are to a listener.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Grammar was the second surprise. Signed languages use the space in front of the signer as a grammatical resource: a person can be placed at a point in that space and referred to later by pointing at it, verbs can move between those points to show who did what to whom, and the face carries grammar rather than only emotion, with particular expressions marking questions, conditions and negation. None of this resembles the grammar of the surrounding spoken language, which is the clearest evidence that signed languages are not translations of speech.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: They are also not universal, which surprises people who assume that gesture is natural. There are well over a hundred signed languages, and the family relationships between them follow the history of schools rather than the history of countries: two signed languages may be closely related because a teacher travelled between the two places, while the spoken languages around them are unrelated. British and American signing, for example, are mutually unintelligible despite a shared spoken language, and Irish signing is closer to French than to either.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The strongest evidence about how languages begin came from a school. When a country that had no deaf education established one, several hundred children who had used only home-made gestures were brought together for the first time. The first cohort developed a shared system that was consistent but limited; the children who arrived a few years later, learning from that first group, produced something with regular grammar that the older group had not had. Successive intakes refined it further, and the process was documented as it happened rather than reconstructed afterwards. Few other cases in linguistics allow a language to be watched arriving, and the case is cited far beyond the study of signing.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Brain studies closed the argument for anyone still holding out. Signing recruits the same regions that speech does, including those associated with the sequencing of grammar rather than with visual processing, and damage to those regions produces the signing equivalent of the speech disorders long described in hearing patients: a patient may lose grammar while retaining the ability to gesture, which is precisely the dissociation the older view predicted could not exist.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Recognition has been slow and uneven. Signed languages were banned from many schools for a century after an international congress in 1880 recommended teaching by speech alone, a decision whose effects on education are still being measured. Legal recognition arrived in a number of countries only in the past two decades, and recognition on paper does not by itself supply interpreters, teacher training or television access, which are what the recognition was sought for.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The practical questions now are about transmission. Most deaf children are born to hearing parents, so the language is usually not passed on at home, and it is learned at school, at clubs, or late; where schools close or move to individual placements, the community that carries the language thins. Technology helps in ways that were not expected: video calling made a signed conversation possible at a distance for the first time, and it did more for daily use of these languages than any legal instrument.
paragraphs.label: H
